questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.topic: What The Interpreter Lock Stops
questions.learningObjective: state what the interpreter lock prevents between threads
questions.stem: Every process of the language holds one lock that the running code must take before it does anything. What is that lock there to stop?

options.text: Two threads of one process running a piece of the language's own code at the same instant
Two threads of one process waiting on the same input or output at the same time
options.misconception: believes the lock stops two threads from both waiting on outside work

options.text: Two separate processes reading and writing the same file at the same time
options.misconception: believes the lock is shared between separate processes on one machine

options.text: Two threads of one process holding the same object in memory at once
options.misconception: believes the lock governs which thread may hold an object at all

questions.explanation: The lock is taken and released around the interpreter's own steps, so only one thread of a process is ever executing that language's code at a given instant, which is what makes the interpreter's internal state safe to keep in plain form. It has no effect at all on a thread that is blocked inside the operating system, and it is not shared with any other process, so work that genuinely waits runs on many threads at once and separate processes are untouched by it. The answer stopping two threads from both waiting is the belief to rule out first, because waiting is exactly the situation the lock is released for.
questions.hint: Ask which code the lock actually wraps, and what a thread does while it is not holding it.

questions.topic: What The Interpreter Lock Leaves Alone
questions.learningObjective: state which kinds of work the interpreter lock does not slow down
questions.stem: A program does a long chain of arithmetic, and separately it waits on many slow replies from a network. Which of the two does the interpreter lock leave running in parallel?

options.text: The waiting, because a thread blocked outside the interpreter holds no lock at all
The arithmetic, because the lock lets any one thread run several steps at once
options.misconception: believes the lock lets a single thread take more than one step at a time

options.text: Neither, because the lock is held from the start of one step to the end of the next
options.misconception: believes the lock is held across a whole step rather than around it

options.text: Both, because the lock is only taken when more than one thread has been created
options.misconception: believes the lock depends on how many threads exist in the process

questions.explanation: The lock is released for the whole time a thread is inside the operating system, so a thread waiting on a reply holds nothing and another thread runs in its place, which is why a fan-out of slow network calls finishes in about the time of the slowest one rather than their sum. The arithmetic is the opposite case, because every one of those steps needs the interpreter, so the threads take turns and no amount of extra threads makes that chain shorter. The answer covering both is the belief to rule out first, because the lock's whole purpose is to serialise the interpreter's own steps and nothing else.
questions.hint: Ask where each of the two spends its time: inside the interpreter, or outside it.

questions.topic: Why A Pool Of Processes Needs Bytes
questions.learningObjective: state why work sent to another process has to be converted before it can go
questions.stem: A pool of processes cannot see the objects of the process that built it. What has to happen to a piece of work before the pool can run it?

options.text: The callable and its values are turned into bytes, written across, and read back on the far side
The callable and its values are shared by reference, so both sides see the same objects
options.misconception: believes two processes share one heap and can pass objects by reference

options.text: The callable and its values are copied field by field into a table the far side can read
options.misconception: believes objects travel as structured field copies rather than as bytes

options.text: Nothing, because the pool runs each task inside the process that submitted it
options.misconception: believes a pool of processes still runs the work in the submitting process

questions.explanation: A separate process has its own memory and its own interpreter, so the only thing that can cross between them is a stream of bytes, and the callable together with everything it needs has to be written as one and read as one. That is why a callable defined inside another function cannot be sent, because there is no way to write down where it lives, and it is also why anything a task passes back comes back as a rebuilt copy rather than the same object. The answer passing by reference is the belief to rule out first, because a reference is an address in one process's memory and means nothing in another.
questions.hint: Ask what a second process can receive, and what would have to happen to an object to become that.

questions.learningObjective: state which part of a piece of work a lock makes indivisible
questions.stem: A thread reads a shared number, adds one to it and writes it back, and a lock is wrapped around those three lines. What does the lock make indivisible?

Only the write, because a read never changes anything another thread can observe
options.misconception: believes a read cannot be observed by another thread and so needs no lock

options.text: The whole function that contains those three lines, including anything it calls
options.misconception: believes a lock covers the entire call rather than the guarded region

options.misconception: believes the interpreter's lock makes a read-add-write sequence atomic

The read matters as much as the write, because a read that happens between another thread's read and its write sees a value that is about to change, and it is that interleaving rather than any single step that loses updates. The answer claiming the whole function is covered is the belief to rule out first, because anything the guarded lines call runs while the lock is held and will serialise too, which is one of the ways a lock turns into a bottleneck.

options.misconception: believes a signal carries the new state and removes the need to re-test

options.text: It promised that the waiter now owns the lock, so it can read the state without taking it

questions.topic: What Separates Waiting Work From Computing Work
questions.learningObjective: state the distinction that decides whether threads or processes suit a workload
questions.stem: One task spends its time multiplying large numbers, and another spends its time waiting for a slow reply from a service. Which task is the one threads suit?

options.text: The one waiting, because waiting happens outside the interpreter and so lets other threads run
The one multiplying, because each thread is given its own interpreter to compute in
options.misconception: believes a thread carries its own copy of the interpreter

options.text: Both, because a thread pool always divides the work between however many threads were asked for
options.misconception: believes the number of threads alone decides how fast work runs

options.text: Neither, because threads only help when the work can be written as one long chain
options.misconception: believes threads need a single chain of work rather than independent pieces

questions.explanation: The useful question is where the time goes. Time spent multiplying belongs to the interpreter, so the threads take turns over it and the wall-clock cost is unchanged however many there are, and the answer there is separate processes because each gets its own interpreter and its own memory. The answer dividing work because a pool was asked for a count is the belief to rule out first, because a pool is a way of handing out work, not a way of making the interpreter do two things at once.
questions.hint: Ask where each task spends its time, inside the interpreter or outside it.

questions.topic: What A Health Check Should Prove
questions.learningObjective: state what a single instance's health check should and should not verify
questions.stem: A service exposes one endpoint that a supervisor calls to decide whether to send it traffic. What should that endpoint check?

options.text: Whether this instance can still do its own work, and leave the whole system to separate checks
Whether every service it depends on answers, so one check covers the whole system
options.misconception: believes one instance's check should trace the whole dependency graph

options.text: Whether the process is running, and nothing else, since that is all a supervisor can act on
options.misconception: believes running at all is the same as being able to serve

options.text: Whether the last request it served succeeded, since one bad reply means the instance is broken
options.misconception: believes a single failed request is enough evidence to fail an instance

The answer tracing the whole graph is the belief to rule out first, because a check that can be failed by something outside the instance has stopped being a statement about the instance.
questions.hint: Ask who acts on the answer, and whether a dependency's trouble should be able to remove this instance.

questions.stem:
Two threads each add to one shared counter and every addition is wrapped in a lock, and the program waits for both threads before printing. What does this program print?

import threading

count = 0
guard = threading.Lock()

def bump(n):
    global count
    for _ in range(n):
        with guard:
            count += 1

threads = [threading.Thread(target=bump, args=(100,)) for _ in range(2)]
for t in threads:
    t.start()
for t in threads:
    t.join()
print(count)

200, because the two threads were never able to be running at the same instant

options.misconception: believes a lock can still lose an update to a shared counter

options.text: 100, because only the thread that finished first added anything to the counter
options.misconception: believes the second thread's additions are dropped when both threads run

questions.explanation: Each thread adds one hundred times and the lock keeps the read, the addition and the write of each of those in one piece, so no addition can be overwritten between another thread's read and its write, and the total is both threads' work added together. questions.topic: What A Condition Variable Wakes
questions.learningObjective: trace one thread waiting on a condition until another signals and fills the shared list
questions.stem:
One thread waits until a shared list is no longer empty and another fills that list and signals, and a short pause before the signal keeps the order of the reports fixed. What does this program print?

import threading
import time

items = []
ready = threading.Condition()
log = []
started = threading.Event()

def add(v):
    with ready:
        items.append(v)
        log.append('added')
        ready.notify_all()

def take():
    with ready:
        started.set()
        while not items:
            log.append('waiting')
            ready.wait()
        log.append('woke')
        items.pop(0)

t = threading.Thread(target=take)
t.start()
started.wait()
time.sleep(0.05)
add('x')
t.join()
print(log, items)

waiting, added, woke and a list holding the item, because waking inspects without taking
options.misconception: believes a woken thread reads the shared state without removing from it

options.text: added, woke and an empty list, because the wait report is skipped when an item is there
options.misconception: believes the waiting report is left out when the item arrived before the wait

options.text: waiting, added, woke and an empty list, then a fault, because waking twice is refused
options.misconception: believes a signal wakes the waiter more than once and the second wake fails

That thread appends the item, records the addition and signals, which wakes the waiter, which re-tests its own condition, finds the list no longer empty, records that it woke and takes the item, leaving the list empty. questions.stem:
Three tasks are handed to a pool and each takes a different amount of time, so they finish in the reverse of the order they were given, and the results are collected by one call. What does this program print?

import time
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

def work(n):
    time.sleep(0.02 * (3 - n))
    return n * 10

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.topic: Why Threads Do Not Help Arithmetic
questions.learningObjective: explain what the interpreter lock does to a chain of arithmetic and why more threads do not shorten it
questions.stem: A service is slow and a team splits one long chain of arithmetic across a growing number of threads, and nothing changes. Explain why that is what happens, and what would have to be different for it to change.

answer.exemplar: Every process of the language holds one lock, and the interpreter takes it around each of its own steps, so at any instant at most one thread of that process is executing a piece of the language's code. That is not a bug and it is not there to make the language slow; it is what allows the interpreter to keep its own bookkeeping in plain form instead of paying for atomic access to it at every step. The consequence is arithmetic. A chain of arithmetic is nothing but interpreter steps, so splitting it across threads means the threads take turns over the same steps and the total work is the same, which is why the wall-clock time does not move as threads are added and why adding more threads can make it worse, because the cost of handing the interpreter over grows while the work being handed over shrinks. The rule to take away is that a thread is a way of overlapping waiting, not a way of overlapping computation. Time spent blocked inside the operating system is time during which the thread holds no lock, so another thread runs, and a fan-out of slow calls finishes in about the time of the slowest one rather than the sum of them. That is the case threads are for. What has to be different for the arithmetic is that it must stop needing the interpreter, and the three ways to arrange that are worth knowing. Put it in another process, since a separate process has its own interpreter and its own lock and the operating system really does run them on different cores. Move it out of the language altogether, into a library built for the work, which is often the cheapest answer when such a library exists. Or change the algorithm so it does less work, which is the only answer that helps a single process and is usually the one worth trying first. The order of preference is worth stating plainly: find out where the time is going before reaching for any of the others, because adding processes to solve a problem that is really an algorithm problem buys memory and start-up cost for nothing.

questions.explanation: The lock is taken around each interpreter step, so a chain of arithmetic is still one step at a time no matter how many threads are waiting to take it, and a thread is a way of overlapping waiting rather than of overlapping computation. The way forward is a separate process with its own interpreter, a library built for the work, or a change of algorithm, and the order of preference is to find the time first.

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.topic: What A Separate Process Buys And Costs
questions.learningObjective: explain what a separate process gives over a thread and what it charges for it
questions.stem: A team can spread a workload across threads or across processes, and the choice is made on speed. Explain what a separate process gains that a thread does not, and what it charges for the gain.

answer.exemplar: The gain is real parallelism and real isolation, and they come from the same source. A process has its own interpreter and therefore its own lock, and the operating system can put two of them on two cores at the same time, so two processes doing arithmetic are genuinely adding. A thread cannot do that, because both threads share one interpreter and one lock. The same boundary that gives the parallelism also isolates the memory, so a crash or a runaway allocation in one process leaves the others running, and a data structure one process built is invisible to the others, which is a safety property and a nuisance at the same time. The costs are concentrated in that boundary, and they are worth naming one at a time. Starting a process is far more expensive than starting a thread, because a whole interpreter and everything it loads has to be brought up, so a workload of many small tasks is dominated by start-up and the design has to batch the work to survive. Anything crossing the boundary has to be turned into bytes and rebuilt on the other side, which is a real cost per crossing and a hard limit on what can cross at all, because a callable defined inside a function has no name to be found by. Memory is not shared either, so a caller that wanted to look at a large structure the worker built has to pay to have it written out and read back. Debugging and profiling get harder, since a stack in one process says nothing directly about the other, and a fault in a worker arrives as a value rather than as a stack. Interrupting a process is blunter than interrupting a thread, which matters for a service that has to shut down promptly. The practical conclusion is that the choice is not between fast and slow but between two kinds of work. A workload that is mostly waiting does not need a process at all, because a thread already overlaps waiting, and a thread is much cheaper to start. A workload that is mostly computing needs a process, because that is the only thing that gives real parallelism, and it needs the work batched into pieces big enough to pay for the trip across. Some services do both, with processes for the heavy part and a small number of threads to feed them, and the boundary is drawn so that the expensive crossing happens as rarely as possible.

questions.explanation: A process has its own interpreter and its own lock, so the operating system can really run two of them at once and a fault in one leaves the others standing, which is what a thread cannot give. It charges for that with an expensive start-up, a write-and-rebuild for anything that crosses, no shared memory, and blunter interruption, so the work has to be batched to pay for the crossing and a workload that is mostly waiting is better served by a cheaper thread.

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.topic: Why A Cache Needs Something To Forget
questions.learningObjective: explain what a cache is buying, what it is risking, and the choices for retiring an entry
questions.stem: A service adds a cache in front of an expensive lookup and the numbers improve, and then something is served that is out of date. Explain what the cache is buying and risking, and the choices available for retiring what it holds.

answer.exemplar: What the cache is buying is the avoidance of a cost. If the underlying lookup takes two hundred milliseconds and the same key is asked for a thousand times a minute, then remembering the answer turns a thousand expensive calls into one and a thousand cheap ones, and that is why the numbers move. What it is risking is that the copy and the original drift apart, and the failure has a particular shape worth naming because it is quiet: the service does not stop working, it starts working on old information, and the only symptom is a user saying a thing they just changed has not changed. Three choices for retiring an entry exist, and they differ in what they assume. Expiring by age is the simplest, and it bounds how wrong a value can be by giving every entry the same lifetime, which is easy to reason about and crude to tune, since a key that changes every second and a key that never changes get the same treatment. Invalidating on write is exact, and it is the only one of the three that can promise a read never returns something the writer has already replaced, but it needs a path from the write to the cache, and if the write happens in another process or another service then that path may not exist. Validating on read sits in between: keep the entry, remember how it was obtained, and on the next read check whether that is still true, which costs something on every read and is only worth it when a read is cheaper than the original lookup. Two practical points go with these. The first is that a cache without a bound is a memory leak wearing a helpful name, because keys arrive from outside and the number of distinct keys is not something the cache controls, so a bounded number of entries or a bounded total size is part of the design rather than an optimisation. The second is that a cache changes the answer to a question the program is already asking, and it should be written so that turning it off is one switch, because the day it is suspected of serving something wrong the first question is whether it is at fault and being able to answer that in one edit is worth more than the complexity of making it permanent. The same reasoning applies to a memory cache and a shared cache, and the shared one has one extra hazard: the invalidation signal has to cross a network, so it is delayed, retried and sometimes lost, and a design that assumes it arrived is a design that will eventually be wrong.

questions.explanation: A cache buys the avoidance of a cost and risks serving a copy that has drifted from its original, quietly, and the three ways out are expiring by age, invalidating on write, and validating on read, each trading exactness for cost. A cache also needs a bound, because the number of distinct keys is not the cache's to control, and it needs a switch that turns it off in one edit.
questions.hint: Ask what the cache avoids, what it can serve instead, and who tells it when the original changed.

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.topic: Finding Out Why A Long Process Grows
questions.learningObjective: explain what makes a long-running process grow and how to find out which it is
questions.stem: A service that has run for a week is using far more memory than it did on its first day, and nothing in its code obviously accumulates. Explain the ways this happens and how to tell which one is happening.

answer.exemplar: There are four shapes this takes, and they are worth listing in the order of how often they turn out to be the answer. The first is a collection that is only ever added to: a list of records, a set of identifiers, a dictionary of results, a log kept in memory because writing it out felt slower. Nothing in this looks like a leak because every line of the code does something sensible, and the growth is only visible as a number that keeps climbing. The fix is to bound it or to move it out of memory, and the test of which is to look at the size of one collection rather than at the whole process. The second is a reference cycle: two things that point at each other, or a thing that points at something that points back, so neither ever reaches a count of zero and neither is reclaimed by plain counting. The collector exists for this and does handle it, so a cycle by itself is usually not the cause, though cycles of a particular shape or objects with their own finalisation can be reclaimed later than expected. The third is a name nobody noticed: a loop's own name outlives the loop and holds its last value, a default argument holding a growing list, a closure holding more than it needs, an exception kept in a traceback that some structure still references. This is the one that most often turns out to be the answer, because the holding reference is a single name in a function nobody has read since it was written. The fourth is fragmentation: the process is not holding more than it needs, but the space it has taken is not being returned to the system, so the number on the dashboard rises while the count of live objects stays flat. Finding out which one is happening comes down to measurement, in a particular order. Take two readings a long way apart and compare them, because a one-off reading tells you nothing. Then compare the number of live objects against the space used, because a rising count of objects points at the first three and a flat count with rising space points at fragmentation. Then look at what kinds of things the live objects are, because the type and the size of the growing group usually names the collection responsible without anybody having to guess. Only after that is it worth reading code, and it is worth reading the code that ran between the two readings. Two things are worth saying about the habits this encourages. Measuring on a schedule catches growth while it is small, because a process that doubles overnight and a process that doubles every hour look identical at the end of the day and completely different at the start. And a bound is a better answer than a diagnosis in a surprising number of cases, because a collection that is allowed to hold at most a fixed number of entries cannot grow without anybody having to find the code that grows it.

questions.explanation: A long-running process grows because a collection is only added to, because two things point at each other, because one name quietly holds a value, or because the space is not being handed back even though the live count is flat, and telling them apart means comparing two readings a long way apart and then comparing the count of live objects against the space used. Measuring on a schedule catches growth while it is small, and a bound is often a better answer than a diagnosis.
questions.hint: Ask whether the count of live objects is rising, and if it is not, what the space is being used for.

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.topic: What A Stop And A Rolling Change Each Promise
questions.learningObjective: explain what a graceful stop and a rolling change guarantee, and what each leaves uncovered
questions.stem: A service is being replaced without a gap in service, and each old instance is given time to finish what it has. Explain what those two arrangements each guarantee and what neither of them covers.

answer.exemplar: The two arrangements are usually described together and they are two different guarantees that happen to fit the same plan. The graceful stop is a statement about one instance and about work in its hands. When the signal arrives the instance stops being offered new work, finishes what it has already accepted, and only then exits, so the guarantee is that no request which was accepted is cut in half. That guarantee has to be bounded, because a request that never finishes would otherwise keep the instance alive for ever, so a limit is set and anything still running at the limit is abandoned rather than waited on, which means the stop does not in fact guarantee that everything finishes. The rolling change is a statement about the service as a whole. A fresh instance is brought up and checked, and only once it passes is an old instance removed, so at every moment during the change there is at least one instance able to serve, and a change that fails its check simply never goes live. That is the guarantee: no gap in service, and a bad change caught before it reaches anybody. What the two together do not cover is worth saying plainly, because these are the situations that produce the incidents people remember. A request that arrives during the change may be served by either version, so a caller cannot assume one behaviour, and a piece of work split across two calls may be handled by two different versions of the code. A change that alters the shape of stored data breaks the instances still running the other version, which is why a rolling change demands that the two versions read each other's data and that the shape be changed in steps rather than in one. A change to a secret read while the program starts does not reach the instances already running, so those keep the old value until they are replaced, and a rotation therefore takes effect gradually rather than at once. A graceful stop given too little time abandons the work it was meant to finish, and one given too much delays the change for everybody. And neither arrangement does anything about a change that is correct for a while and then degrades, because every check in the plan happens at the start. The practical conclusion is that both arrangements buy continuity and both charge for it in overlap, so the work that remains is to make the overlap survivable: the two versions must be able to live together, the data they share must be readable by both, and the limit on the drain has to be a number somebody chose rather than a number nobody wrote down.

questions.explanation: A graceful stop guarantees that work already accepted is not cut in half, and a rolling change guarantees that something is always serving and that a change failing its check never goes live. Neither covers the overlap: during a change a request may be served by either version, a change to stored data or to a secret only reaches instances as they are replaced, and a drain with too small a limit abandons the work it was meant to finish.
questions.hint: Ask what is true of the service during the change, and what happens to a request that arrives mid-change.

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.topic: What A Report Needs To Be Worth Reading
questions.learningObjective: explain what makes a captured failure report actionable rather than merely recorded
questions.stem: A service reports its failures to a tracker automatically, and the reports arrive faster than anyone can read them. Explain what a report has to carry for it to be worth reading, and what usually makes reports unusable.

answer.exemplar: A report is worth reading if it tells someone what to do next, and almost everything that goes wrong is the failure of one of those requirements. The first is identification: something that says which service, which version and which instance, because a stack from an unidentified instance cannot be matched to a change and a stack from the wrong version cannot be reasoned about at all. The second is the request that caused it, or as much of the request as may safely be kept, because a failure that cannot be tied to an input cannot be reproduced and a failure that cannot be reproduced cannot be fixed with confidence. The third is what the service was doing at the time, which is the surrounding work rather than the fault itself: what it had been asked for, how long it had been running, what it had been waiting on. The fourth is the sequence, because most real failures are a chain rather than a moment, and the interesting line is often the one that happened well before the one that was reported. The fifth is grouping, which is a property of the system rather than of the report: a thousand copies of one fault should be one entry with a count, or the queue that people work through never gets shorter. Two things make reports unusable and both are common. The first is losing the context that made the failure meaningful, usually because a piece of the request was dropped for being too large or was considered sensitive, which leaves a report that says a thing went wrong and nothing about what it was working on. The second is reporting the wrong thing: an exception that was raised, caught and handled somewhere below, or a message from a library that has been read by nobody who knows what it means, both of which turn a real signal into noise. The advice that follows is short. Decide the fields before the first report is written, because adding one later means finding every place a report is produced. Keep the request, keep the stack, and keep the identifiers, and treat anything that would let somebody act as that customer as something to be handled deliberately rather than dropped by accident. Make sure one report of one failure is one entry, so that a fault seen ten thousand times is one thing to look at rather than ten thousand. And keep a report from a healthy service, because the ratio between reports and successes is the number that says whether anything is wrong, and a report that only appears when something has already broken has lost the half of the signal that would have said it was coming.

questions.explanation: A report is worth reading if it names the service, version and instance, carries the request that caused the failure, says what the service was doing at the time, keeps the sequence leading up to it, and groups repeats of one fault into one entry, and it goes unread when the context is dropped or when handled exceptions are reported as if they were failures. The fields have to be decided before the first report is written, and healthy periods have to be reported too.
questions.hint: Ask whether the report says what to do next, and whether a person could match it to a change and reproduce it.

done = [0]
